newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan gold demand seen slipping further in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Japan gold demand seen slipping further in 1997.

text.p: Japan's gold demand is expected to fall a bit further in 1997 from last year's already depressed levels, with jewellery sales likely to keep slumping and investors still shunning the market, industry sources say.

They said an expected slowdown in the economy's recovery this year, due in part to this April's scheduled sales tax increase and an end to special tax cuts, could deal yet another blow to the battered jewellery market.

"As for gold demand this year, we cannot become optimistic, as in my view the worst is not yet over for gold demand from the jewellery sector," said Makoto Tonoki, general manager at Tanaka Kikinzoku Kogyo KK, Japan's largest bullion house.
"Amid uncertainty over the economy, luxury items such as jewellery would be the last thing consumers would buy," he told Reuters,
Japan's gold imports in the first 11 months of 1996, at 126.30 tonnes, were barely half the 249.67 tonnes imported in the same period the year before, Finance Ministry data showed.
A recent report by Tanaka Kikinzoku estimated that Japan's gold jewellery demand fell to 80 tonnes in 1996 from 86 tonnes the year before.
Gold demand from Japanese investors, while highly volatile, was also not seen recovering anytime soon. Japan is traditionally one of the world's largest consumers of gold.

Last year investment demand fell sharply from the year before, partly because the yen's depreciation against the dollar boosted local yen-based prices. Japanese investors tend to step into the market when they feel gold prices are cheap.
The Tanaka report estimated last year's investment demand for gold at 90 tonnes, only half the 181 tonnes in 1995.
Industry sources said, however, that 1995 was an unusual year for investor demand, as the Kobe earthquake and a series of banking crises scared some investors into buying gold as a safe haven.
Last year brought no such domestic catastrophes, however, and many of the investors who bought gold in 1995 decided to sell it off and take profits in 1996.

In 1997, traders said, Japanese investor demand will hinge on yen-based retail prices, but at this stage demand is unlikely to be lifted by the sharp drop in dollar-based gold prices since the start of this year, as it has been offset by the yen's weakening against the dollar.

"Yen-based gold prices remain at high levels. Unless retail prices fall below 1,200 yen ($10) per gram, a significant rise in gold investment demand is unlikely," said Yukuji Sonoda of Sumisho Gold Co Ltd.
Yen-based retail gold prices are currently around 1,370 ($11.81) yen per gram, up from the 20-year low of 1,070 yen ($9.22) marked on May 29, 1994.

Gold's lacklustre price performance over the past year has also cooled consumer interest in gold savings plans, which had attracted many small investors to the gold market in the past few years. ($1=116 yen)
